cues.text: A New Faith in Buganda

Catholic missionaries known as the White Fathers arrived in the kingdom of Buganda, in what is now Uganda, in 1879, welcomed by King Mutesa I, who tolerated Catholic, Protestant, and Muslim missionaries alike among his people.
Among the earliest and most promising converts were young men serving as royal pages in the king's own court, learning the Catholic faith even as they continued their palace duties.
A New King, A New Danger
When Mutesa died in 1884, his teenage son Mwanga II inherited the throne.
He grew increasingly hostile toward the Christians in his household, viewing their growing numbers and moral resistance to his conduct as a direct threat to his authority.
Joseph Mukasa, the Catholic head of the royal pages, was beheaded in November 1885 after openly denouncing the king’s murder of a visiting Anglican bishop.
He was also beheaded for his efforts to shield the younger pages under his charge from the king’s abuses.
Charles Lwanga Steps Forward
On the very night of Mukasa's execution, Charles Lwanga , a twenty-five-year-old page, sought and received baptism.
Already respected for leadership among the boys, he took up Mukasa's role as protector of the younger pages in the royal household.
He continued instructing them in the faith and shielding them from the king's demands, even at growing personal risk.
'Until Death'
In May 1886, Mwanga discovered that pages under his authority were still receiving Christian instruction.
Enraged, he had the entire company of pages assembled and demanded to know who among them intended to remain Christian.
Fifteen young men and boys, ranging in age from about thirteen to twenty-five, stepped forward and answered as one: "Until death!"
The Fires of Namugongo

The condemned were marched roughly forty miles to Namugongo , several killed along the way, before being wrapped in reed mats and burned alive together on 3 June 1886 — the Feast of the Ascension that year.
Charles Lwanga was separated out and burned alone first.
He is reported to have told his executioners that it felt 'as if you are pouring water over my body.'
The fire was lit slowly to prolong his suffering.
He is reported to have died crying out 'Katonda!'
— 'My God!'
His companions, among them the fourteen-year-old Kizito, whom Lwanga had personally baptized in prison, died together singing hymns.
Legacy
Persecution continued for months afterward, ultimately claiming twenty-two Catholic martyrs alongside a comparable number of Anglican Christians killed for the same refusal to abandon their faith.

Rather than extinguishing Christianity in Uganda, the persecution had the opposite effect: when missionaries were permitted to return after Mwanga's eventual downfall, they found the Christian community had grown nearly fourfold in secret.
Pope Paul VI canonized Charles Lwanga and his companions together in 1964, making them the first martyrs of sub-Saharan Africa so honored.
They are commemorated each year at the Basilica of the Uganda Martyrs in Namugongo, now one of the world's largest annual Catholic pilgrimage gatherings.
